paragraphs.text: In the dry south of the country, a research farm has been testing ways to grow vegetables with very little fresh water. The project began in 2016 after two years of drought left many local farmers without an income.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The farm’s greenhouses are cooled by seawater, which is pumped from the coast and trickled over cardboard panels. As the water evaporates, the air inside becomes cooler and more humid, so plants lose less moisture through their leaves.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Some of the evaporated water is collected again as it condenses on cold pipes, providing fresh water for irrigation. The system produces around 5,000 litres a day, enough for roughly a hectare of tomatoes.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Energy for the pumps comes from solar panels on the greenhouse roofs. Engineers first placed the panels over the whole roof, but tomato yields fell because the plants received too little light, and the panels now cover only one side.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The researchers are cautious about the cost. Building a greenhouse of this kind is still more expensive than a conventional one, and the method only works close to the sea. Nevertheless, several local farmers have visited the site, and two have asked for help in building smaller versions.
paragraphs.label: E

a design change made after a disappointing result
